title: How to Count Days in a TREC Contract
title_html: How to Count Days in a TREC Contract
meta_title: How to Count Days in a TREC Contract — Texas Real Estate
meta_description: How to count days in a Texas TREC contract: Effective Date is day zero, calendar days only, and the ¶ 5A(2) weekend/holiday rollover that applies only to earnest money and the option fee.
deck: The single most-miscounted concept in Texas residential contracts.
calculator_blurb: Verify your day-counts against the calculator below — it implements the rules described in this guide exactly.
related_blurb: How to count to a TREC deadline correctly — the off-by-one that costs deals.
body_html:
Counting days in a Texas residential contract sounds simple. It is not. Three rules collide, and getting any one wrong puts a deadline on the wrong day. Here's how to count correctly.

Rule 1: Effective Date is day zero

The Effective Date is the date the last party signs and delivery occurs. It isn't a numbered paragraph — it's defined in the unnumbered execution/signature block ("EXECUTED the ___ day of ___, 20__ (Effective Date)"). When ¶ 5A says "within 3 days after the Effective Date," the Effective Date itself isn't day 1 — it's day zero. Day 1 is the day after.

Example: Effective Date is Monday May 4. The earnest money deadline (3 days) is Thursday May 7, not Wednesday.

Rule 2: Calendar days, not business days

TREC counts calendar days for everything. Weekends are included in the count. Holidays are included in the count. The only place weekends and holidays matter is the rollover rule below.

Example: A 21-day financing deadline starting on Monday May 4 spans three weekends. The 21 days are calendar days — you count straight through Saturdays and Sundays.

Rule 3: ¶ 5A(2) rolls weekend/holiday landings — but only for earnest money and the option fee

If the earnest money, option fee, or additional earnest money deadline lands on a Saturday, Sunday, or Legal Holiday (Texas Government Code §662.003(a), (b)(4), (b)(6) — includes Juneteenth and the Friday after Thanksgiving, neither of which is a federal holiday), ¶ 5A(2) rolls it forward to the next day that isn't one of those. Title objection, survey, financing, and closing deadlines are fixed calendar dates and don't roll.

Example: Effective Date Monday May 4. Earnest money is 3 days → Thursday May 7. No rollover needed. Financing is 21 days → Monday May 25, which happens to be Memorial Day — but financing deadlines don't roll under ¶ 5A(2), so the deadline stays Monday May 25 even though it's a holiday.

What actually doesn't roll: ¶ 5B (the option period) is one of several TREC deadlines that do not roll for weekends or holidays — alongside title objection, survey, financing, and closing. Only earnest money, the option fee, and additional earnest money roll, under ¶ 5A(2). Even if the option period ends on a Saturday or a federal holiday, the buyer must deliver any termination notice by 5:00 PM on that exact day. There is no Monday extension, no day-after-Christmas grace period.

What "5:00 PM" actually means

Most TREC notice deadlines (option period, financing notice, etc.) cite 5:00 PM as the cutoff. That's 5:00 PM local to the property, not local to the agent or the lender. For a property in Austin, the deadline is 5:00 PM Central. For a property in El Paso, that part of Texas observes Mountain Time — 5:00 PM Mountain is 6:00 PM Central. If you're a Dallas agent representing a buyer on an El Paso property, set your reminder to 5:00 PM in El Paso, not in Dallas.

Putting it together: a worked example

Effective Date Friday May 1, 2026. Closing date Monday June 1, 2026. 7-day option, 3-day earnest money, 3-day option fee, 21-day financing, 10-day survey.

Earnest money (¶ 5A)5/1 + 3Mon 5/4Mon 5/4
Option fee (¶ 5A)5/1 + 3Mon 5/4Mon 5/4
Option period (¶ 5B)5/1 + 7Fri 5/8Fri 5/8 by 5pm — never rolls
Survey (¶ 6C)5/1 + 10Mon 5/11Mon 5/11
Financing (40-11)5/1 + 21Fri 5/22Fri 5/22
Closing (¶ 9A)—Mon 6/1Mon 6/1

Why agents miscount

The most common errors:

  1. Off-by-one on Effective Date. Treating it as day 1 when it's day 0 makes every deadline a day too early.
  2. Counting business days for the option period. Calendar days, including weekends.
  3. Applying rollover to deadlines that don't get it. Only earnest money, the option fee, and additional earnest money roll under ¶ 5A(2) — title, survey, financing, closing, and the option period (¶ 5B) are fixed calendar dates.
  4. Forgetting the property-local time zone. 5:00 PM is local to the property, not your office.

The calculator below applies all of these rules exactly — including the option-period non-rollover and the property-local 5:00 PM convention. Use it on every deal until the math becomes second nature.

faq.q: Is the Effective Date the same as the contract date?
faq.a: No. The Effective Date is the date the last party signs AND delivery occurs — typically the day the executed contract is acknowledged in writing back to the other party. It isn't defined in a numbered paragraph; it's set by the unnumbered execution/signature block ("EXECUTED the ___ day of ___, 20__ (Effective Date)"). The contract date (the date written in the form) is often earlier.

faq.q: Do I count Saturday and Sunday in the option period?
faq.a: Yes. Calendar days, weekends included. A 7-day option that starts on Friday ends the next Friday — you count straight through both weekend days.

faq.q: What if the option period ends on Christmas Day?
faq.a: The option period still expires that day at 5:00 PM. ¶ 5B does not roll. If you suspect this could happen on a deal, negotiate a longer option or pre-deliver the inspection schedule before the holiday.

faq.q: Does ¶ 5A(2)'s rollover apply to the closing date?
faq.a: No. ¶ 5A(2)'s rollover rule is scoped to earnest money, the option fee, and additional earnest money only. The closing date itself is a specific calendar date set in ¶ 9A. If that date lands on a federal holiday, parties typically agree to move closing — but it's a matter of practice and title-company availability, not an automatic rollover.

faq.q: Are Texas state holidays counted as rollover days?
faq.a: No, not exactly. ¶ 5A(2) references "Legal Holiday" as defined by Texas Government Code §662.003(a), (b)(4), and (b)(6) — not federal holidays. That list is close to the federal list but adds Juneteenth and the Friday after Thanksgiving, both of which trigger rollover even though neither is a federal holiday. Other Texas state holidays (Confederate Heroes Day, Texas Independence Day) fall outside that statutory list, so they are not treated as rollover days for the earnest money and option fee deadlines that ¶ 5A(2) covers.
